results.content: SOTA Coding Agents: High-Octane Productivity or High-Maintenance Coworkers? 🚀 I've been spending a lot of time lately with state-of-the-art coding agents. My first impression? It's a mix bag - highly productive, yet deeply frustrating. We are living in a world where we can move faster, but we have to spend m "babysitting" the agent. The Wins (Where they shine): ✅ Context at Scale: Ramping up on a new codebase or area is significantly faster. ✅ The "Grunt Work": They are masters at adding debug prints, assertions, or commenting out code across multiple files in seconds. ✅ Log Sifting: They can analyze massive outputs and extract the "signal from the noise" almost instantly. ✅ Snippet Speed: Great for generating small-to-medium utility functions on the fly. The Friction (The "Shortfalls"): [...] Write Better Code Faster Without Losing Control Speed is great. Control is better. The best engineers know you don't have to sacrifice one for the other. One of the most common productivity killers I see today is vague prompts, especially when using AI or collaborating with other developers. Bad Practice "Fix this function." What does "fix" mean? - Is it broken? - Is it slow? - Is it unreadable? - Are we allowed to change behavior? This kind of prompt hands over all decision-making and increases the risk of unintended changes. Better practice: Think like an engineer, prompt like one Instead of vague instructions, give clear constraints and intent: You are a senior software engineer (attach a programming language or framework you are using). Refactor this function to: - Improve [...] STOP CODING. I resisted this for months. Decades of muscle memory said my value was in the code I wrote. I was wrong. In 2026, coding by hand is counterproductive. The leverage isn't in typing faster or knowing more syntax. It's in engineering and architecting solutions - then letting AI write the implementation. Once I made that shift, I became 100x more productive. Not exaggeration. Production-ready applications, shipped, that would have taken teams months. This is where asymmetric advantage lives now. Not in writing code. In directing code. I've been exploring agentic coding with Claude Code - treating prompts as engineering artifacts, not throwaway instructions. results.title: Coding agents are giving everyone decision fatigue
results.content:
There's a reason people who make a lot of decisions, like presidents and CEOs, wear the same thing every day: one less decision. They build processes around gathering the information, utilizing multiple layers of experts and trust, hopefully building multiple checks and verifications before they make consequential decisions. Judgement is a skill and a process, and good decisions come from context and experience. Experience, as the joke goes, comes from bad decisions. [...] ## Every builder is a decider

Smartsheet's research found that 80% of AI-generated content is edited before it's finalized. Those edits come from getting an understanding of the context of that code (or other content). For AI-generated code, no one wrote the original code, so the context you need to gather is greater. You can look at prompts, specs, and whatever other context your agent uses, but that's a lot of work to produce a judgement. If we're shifting the majority of software work from coding to making decisions, everyone is going to feel the strain of decision fatigue.
